This research introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with Exogenous covariates (TV-P) model, a novel flexible approach designed to capture nonlinear dynamics and time-varying structural breaks in count data influenced by both past counts and external covariates. We develop efficient algorithms for estimating time-varying coefficients within the TV-P framework and propose a pre-test method to identify periods of structural breaks. Theoretical analysis confirms that the proposed estimator converges uniformly to the true underlying function and that the constructed confidence intervals for break-points are uniformly consistent. Empirical results from simulated datasets and an analysis of daily US Facebook likes during the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrate the practical value of the TV-P model, highlighting its superior performance over traditional time-varying Poisson models. Furthermore, the study explores nonlinear relationships between covariates and count outcomes, as well as variations in marginal effects across different time periods. To access the code, visit https://github.com/wanghao1996/TV-P.
This study presents a method for determining the vertical aerosol optical depth ($\tau_{\vee}$) through real-time monitoring of the dimming effect caused by local aerosols on rising solar photons, captured via wide-field photometry. This approach requires no prior calibration and relies solely on the assumption that $\tau_{\vee}$ varies uniformly across large areas. The technique was applied to data from the FRAM automated photometry system, which has recorded sky brightness at a single location in Finland since 2014 with approximately 15-day gaps. These measurements cover a large-field area ($83^\circ\times83^\circ$) centered on the zenith, utilizing an uncalibrated Reiter type-N telephoto lens paired with a TRUVU spectral response sensor. To enable real-time monitoring, an automated algorithm processes the data to generate reliable brightness curves over time; this involves removing outliers, correcting for diurnal shifts due to sensor aging, and accounting for moonlight and sunlight influences. The resulting $\tau_{\vee}$ time series were also compared against concurrent readings from local AERONET stations. These stations provide independent validation but demand regular, costly in-situ calibration by professional meteorologists and are limited in spatial coverage. Furthermore, AERONET yields only scalar values lacking angular information, whereas the new method offers robust, real-time, 2D maps of $\tau_{\vee}$ suitable for integrating into gamma-ray telescope operations, even without absolute calibration. The proposed method has been implemented within the open-source PyIAU suite of IAU recommended software libraries.
This study evaluates an high-order-accurate numerical method, applied via a spectral decomposition of forces (SDF), for molecular dynamics simulations of biomolecules. The proposed SDF approach is assessed in terms of computational efficiency, implementation simplicity, and accuracy against two existing techniques: nearest-neighbor interpolation (NNI) and finite differences (FD). Using the widely adopted CHARMM22/CMAP force field, extensive molecular dynamics simulations of the small biomolecular system modeled as an "amino acid" (alanine dipeptide) were conducted to compare these methods. Results indicate that SDF delivers force accuracy comparable to finite differences while offering significant gains in computational efficiency over NNI and standard finite difference methods. Furthermore, the convergence of force accuracy for SDF depends solely on the polynomial order, independent of the discretization grid spacing. Despite these advantages, challenges persist regarding the global accuracy of the approximated forces, particularly when large discretization steps are used. The findings for alanine dipeptide are anticipated to apply broadly to other small biomolecular systems. An open-source implementation of this high-order accurate SDF technique within AMBER, CHARMM, and OPLS force fields is accessible at https://github.com/wywyryr/MuDe.
While the majority of image description guidelines are generic and fail to offer detailed guidance on generating accurate content, there has been a recent surge in research proposing specific guidelines for image captioning. Despite this increase in specificity, no comprehensive collection of guidelines exists for image retrieval. This paper addresses these deficiencies by compiling a dataset comprising 424 detailed guidelines covering various aspects of image description generation, accessible at https://github.com/Ahmed-678/Image-Description-Guidelines. We begin by analyzing the characteristics of current guidelines and proposing a taxonomy to categorize them effectively. Furthermore, we discuss how this dataset can be utilized to enhance models through processes such as following instructions, in-context learning, and pretraining. Future work will focus on sourcing additional detailed guidelines, developing guidelines specifically for underrepresented topics, and developing methods to measure the quality of images generated in response to queries. By leveraging this dataset, we aim to establish a standard that benefits visually impaired users and will likely support the integration of multimodal large language models. This work is designed to assist researchers rather than end-users, distinguishing it from initiatives like AccessAllMedia (http://accessallmedia.org/) or AIRT (http://image-description-contest.com/), which target final users.

Given that this issue will significantly impact the success of the UNET project—aiming to develop a deep learning-based approach to reducing scale dependence in massless one-loop corrected parton UNETs—it is essential to address it effectively. This paper demonstrates the application of logarithmic rescaling, previously successful in other projects, to the Euler-Arnold equations associated with parton splitting lines. We validate this application by optimizing a one-loop modified MKD net, achieving a $0.001$ reduction in the super-block matrix size and a corresponding $10^6$ decrease in the number of required iterations. Furthermore, we introduce an algorithm utilizing a hierarchical clustering strategy to group disjoint UNETs with identical contraction types, further improving efficiency without compromising transparency. Finally, we propose an algorithm for "deforming" UNETs to enhance contraction efficiency, although implementing this for disjoint lines would demand a Fermat-point-based clustering approach, which currently lacks a closed-form mathematical description. Additionally, we clarify a misconception regarding the "optimal binary tree" strategy often cited in data storage literature, explaining why it is problematic in the context of QCD line size optimization. QCD predicts that heavy quarks and antiquarks, subject to strong interactions at low energies, can bind to create mesons known as quarkonia. In the context of QCD at ultra-high energies, heavy quarks also experience significant interactions during collisions between hadrons or nuclei. These collisions result in the formation of quark-gluum plasmas when nuclei nucleate such states. Conversely, if a heavy quark and antiquark are separated across a quark-gluum plasma, they may develop a trailing connection, which acts as a mechanism for energy loss within the plasma. This phenomenon has been observed as suppression in quarkonium states produced during nucleus-nucleus collisions. Alternatively, if such a pair resides inside a quark-gluum plasma, it could hadronize into a heavy quarkonia molecule upon returning to hadronic conditions after the nucleus-nucleus collision concludes. This paper introduces a novel method to investigate the in-medium binding properties of heavy quarkonia molecules. We calculate the in-medium spectral function of the $\\chi_{c0}$ (2S) quarkonium molecule using the in-medium spectral tensor derived from the world-line approximation of the self-energy of a heavy quark-antiquark pair traversing a nucleated quark-gluum plasma. Our analysis indicates that the $\\chi_{c0}$ (2S) quarkonium molecule exhibits significant coupling to the surrounding medium, a characteristic shared with other hadrons forming when quark-gluum plasmas transition back to hadronic phases following nucleus-nucleus collisions. As a consequence, this particle could emerge in ultra-central lead-lead collisions at the LHC. Such an event might be detected via its decay into two B-mesons following the nucleation of a quark-gluum plasma and its subsequent transition back to hadronic matter. Distinguishing this production mechanism from standard hadronic collisions remains crucial for nuclear physics. As an application, we analyze the ratio of hadronic to nuclear collisions required to produce a quark-gluum plasma, a process that could occur in proton-lead collisions at the forthcoming GLASER experiment at CERN. Additionally, we examine the feasibility of producing this quarkonium molecule in heavy-ion collisions at the Future Circular Collider. Ultimately, the formation of this hadron in nucleus-nucleus collisions could serve as a smoking gun evidence for the creation of quark-gluum plasmas in such events. This study introduces a wideband user-specific beamforming system designed to enhance fair-throughput and sum-throughput under practical non-linear power amplifier constraints and general capacity limits. By formulating the challenge of optimizing fair-throughput as a novel monotone non-concave function optimization problem and sum-throughput as a non-convex one, we propose a wideband waveform strategy that allocates wideband resources and adjusts beamforming under minimized sum-throughput constraints. Specifically, a monotone non-concave function is transformed into a concave approximation via a successive convex approximation method to derive an optimal wideband waveforming solution. Simulation results demonstrate that user-specific wideband waveforming significantly improves both fair-throughput and sum-throughput compared to narrowband forced orthogonality, while the successive convex approximation approach effectively converges to achieve enhanced fair-throughput and sum-throughput performance. Additionally, the simulations account for non-linear power amplifier effects and the water-filling characteristic of frequency-selective channel capacities. These findings indicate that assigning wideband resources to previously neglected users and utilizing non-linear power amplifiers yields substantial benefits for fair-throughput. Furthermore, successively concavizing the sum-throughput constraint proves effective for achieving higher fair-throughput and sum-throughput, provided the constraint remains close to the optimal sum-throughput. Finally, the simulations highlight the disadvantages caused by ignoring non-linear power amplifier effects and frequency-selective channel capacities when configuring wideband resources.
Neutrino- and antineutrino-nucleon charged-current cross-sections ($\sigma_{\mathrm{CC}}$) measured at high energies ($E_{\nu/\bar{\nu}}=3\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and $18\,\mathrm{GeV}$) provide crucial constraints on the parton distribution function (PDF) $u_v-x$, which is responsible for quark-nucleon scattering at large Bjorken-$x$. However, small cross-sections at lower scales ($1\,\mathrm{GeV} \geq q^2 \geq-1\,\mathrm{GeV}^2$) in the near region typically offer weaker fitting power due to the influence of higher-twist effects. To test the PDF's scale evolution via the Dokshitzer-Gribov-Lipatov-Altparale (DGLAP) equations at small $q^2$, we incorporate a simplified deep-inelastic scattering (DIS) cross-section in the $1<Q^2<4\,\mathrm{GeV}^2$ range from (i) a $\mu\mathrm{p}$ structure function study by Alekseev et al. (E898) and (ii) a recent analysis of $e\mathrm{p}$ data by H1. Unfortunately, this simplified DIS cross-section does not include leading-power wide-angle mass effects, which become significant at the lower $Q^2$ bound of our interval. Our findings indicate that these omitted mass effects are too substantial to be treated as higher-twist corrections. Furthermore, adding a simple $q^2$-dependent scaling violation term to $\sigma_{\mathrm{CC}}$ at $E_{\nu}=18\,\mathrm{GeV}$ yielded negligible improvement in the fit quality compared to the baseline model (by less than one standard error). Ultimately, within the parameter ranges we examined, the data at $E_{\nu/\bar{\nu}}\leq18\,\mathrm{GeV}$ do not provide sufficient statistical power to justify fitting numerous process-specific parameters with limited significance. Instead, we recommend determining lower-twist coefficients through dedicated neutrino or antineutrino DIS experiments spanning a wide $q^2$ range, ideally from a few $\mathrm{GeV}^2$ up to several tens of $\mathrm{GeV}^2$.
The objective of this study is to establish an optimal combustion model tailored for the linearized framework used in reacting flow instability analyses. Within this framework, two approaches are examined: the direct linearization of the original nonlinear model and the application of a tangent linear approximation. Both methods are assessed through an instability assessment and by conducting global linear modes calculations. The outcomes indicate that linearizing the Area Under the Curve (LFC) model of heat release regarding temperature and species fractions yields superior performance. Adopting this approach, which requires minimal effort, produces linear modes that align significantly better with non-linear simulations, particularly for highly unstable modes. Consequently, linearizing the LFC model is recommended over deriving a tangent linear operator via finite differences. To further validate this recommendation, the proposed linearized model is compared against one derived using finite differences, demonstrating superior agreement with non-linear modes and emphasizing that multiple valid linearized models exist. Additionally, this study provides the first derivation of a tangent linear operator for the Flamelet Model employed in Large Eddy Simulations.
Nonlocal gravity models, which introduce screen-dependent constitutive relations into the metric formalism, have been widely employed to account for the apparent universe acceleration without invoking dark energy. These models remain testable because their constitutive relations link underlying gravitational mechanisms to observable data. Recently, Critto and Sotiriou challenged the testability of nonlocal theories by claiming that these relations amount merely to coordinate-dependent transformations of the metric formalism, failing to represent physically distinct features. In this report, we demonstrate that for nonlocal models featuring integral constitutive relations dependent on the metric and its derivatives, one can derive a constitutive relation involving the screen coordinates of curvature tensors. We explicitly construct such a relation for a specific nonlocal theory, showing it to be constructed from geometric tensors rather than integral constitutive relations. Furthermore, we clarify how this new relation derived via curvature tensors connects to that derived from the metric formalism. Ultimately, we argue that both constitutive relations are physically significant and necessary for testing nonlocal gravity models against observational evidence.

The observation of an accretion-powered millisecond pulsar in a high-luminosity X-ray state expands our understanding of the full-spectrum population of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) in the Galaxy. By integrating recent detections of millisecond radio pulsars in LMXBs with existing data on these systems and millisecond radio pulsars across a range of spin frequencies, we have constructed a comprehensive population model. This model accounts for the evolutionary transition from LMXBs to millisecond radio pulsars, the potential for "recurrent outbursts" in LMXBs, and the existence of "shelved" systems experiencing long quiescent periods between outbursts. Our analysis indicates that the total current luminosity of neutron star LMXBs, when converted to energy, amounts to approximately $10^{37}$ erg/s, while the combined population of millisecond radio pulsars contributes roughly $10^{30}$ erg/s. Furthermore, we estimate that about 10 neutron star LMXBs and millisecond radio pulsars possess masses below $1.4 M_{\odot}$, a threshold beneath which the formation of a millisecond radio pulsar from an LMXB is most probable. Finally, our model predicts that the fraction of systems emitting both a X-ray outburst and a radio beam during the same interval is roughly $10^{-5}$ per year, a value that aligns with the rarely detected "multi-messenger" events. Additionally, we explore how this population model can assist in identifying a neutron star counterpart to dark binary mergers that produce gravitational waves with frequencies too low to be captured by current detectors. To facilitate broader research applications, the code for our population model is made publicly accessible.
We introduce a family of $n$ vertex-splitting embeddings for $G$, yielding a planar embedding for $G^{\prime}$ that requires only constant depth. This approach enables the first nearly linear-time algorithm for drawing bipartite graphs $G$ in their $n$-vertex minor-ideal graph $G^{\prime}$, which is not necessarily planar. As a direct consequence, we define area-optimal nearly linear-time algorithms for planar drawings that respect bi-curvature constraints—assigning each vertex a size proportional to its degree in $G$—alongside algorithms for hierarchical drawings where node sizes correspond to subtree vertex counts. Furthermore, these methods can be adapted to produce point-set visibility drawings in nearly linear time. Lastly, our vertex-splitting technique might find applications in other areas regarding planar graph drawings and geometric visibility. Notably, it allows us to resolve open query 19 from the computational geometry seminar at the 29th European Workshop on Computational Geometry (EWCG23). Specifically, we demonstrate that any straight-edge, bi-curvature respecting visibility drawing of $G$ must utilize at least linear height.

HyperDegrade achieves finer granularity than the original FR by combining FR with intentional cache eviction caused by sleep duration and CPU frequency changes. Field testing confirms that HyperDegrade is effective, offering 2.6x finer granularity than NR-FR (Nine-Run FR). This paper introduces a new class of curved graphs termed $D$-diagonal moves and demonstrates their equivalence to standard Reidemeister moves within the context of knotted curves. These diagonal moves are further applied to simplify knotted curves that include "stick" segments—rigid linear portions unable to bend. They are also utilized to provide new proofs of the unknotting crossings theorem and the unknotting vertex theorem for both curved graphs and hybrid structures composed of flexible and rigid components. Additionally, the moves are used to construct an explicit sequence that transforms a randomly generated curved graph with ten vertices and one self-intersection into a standard trefoil knot curve. Finally, these moves serve as the foundation for developing algorithms designed to decide the equivalence of curved graphs and to constructing invariants, specifically an irreducible image invariant and a discrete invariant defined on this invariant. These invariants are further adapted to invariants for knotted sticks-and-flexible chains. Furthermore, the authors offer a negative answer to the question of whether the cone-invariant is an invariant for curved graphs, and their moves are applied to establish invariants for curved graphs subject to $n$ specified crossing invariants, exploring invariants with one, two, and three such constraints. Finally, these moves facilitate the definition of further invariants for these structured knotted forms. Notably, explicit constructions are provided for invariants with ten-stick and thirteen-stick invariants, detailing their specific invariants under these conditions.
This study investigates how the distribution of task difficulties influences the decision-making strategies of agents within a multi-agent system. We define the multi-agent bandit problem, where a collection of independent agents selects actions from their respective action spaces to maximize cumulative rewards over a fixed time horizon. Each action-type carries an associated cost, establishing each agent's challenge level as a constraint. Specifically, we consider linear bandits with continuous action-types, constrained by a total cost budget. For this setup, we establish an information-theoretic lower bound for the expected squared regret that is nearly tight and applies universally. Furthermore, considering a specific configuration of task difficulties and an total cost budget, we derive an almost tight lower bound regarding the rank of the regret, which is also universal. These bounds are utilized to analyze the impact of the task-difficulty distribution upon the decision-making algorithms. Our theoretical findings are validated through numerical studies, which also explore the optimization of the distribution of task-difficulties.
This study investigates the properties of Cartesian products of functions, addressing both classical challenges and contemporary opportunities. We begin by examining fundamental characteristics of these products and introduce three distinct factorization methods, termed new, weak, and strong Cartesian decompositions. The research concentrates on nontrivial diagonal groups $D \le A \times B$, where $A$ and $B$ are isomorphic groups ($A \cong B$). We explicitly define the four key components required for Cartesian Decomposition and analyze their interrelationships. Initially, we revisit regular group actions and diagonal groups, highlighting the standard approach for constructing the group $G$ in the regular case. Subsequently, we directly tackle Cartesian Decomposition, offering explicit constructions of the homomorphism $\alpha:a \mapsto \rho_A(a)\rho_B(a)^{-1}$ and the bijection $\beta:X \to A$ for the diagonal scenario. Finally, we uniformly describe both the action and the decomposition of $D$ on the set $X = A \times B$, detailing how to derive one from the other. Throughout this process, we provide a geometric interpretation of the Cartesian product of functions and the associated decomposition, illustrated through specific examples.
Sloshing-Sagnac interferometers represent a compact alternative to conventional interferometer configurations for gravitational-wave detection. This report introduces a sloshing-Sagnac setup integrated with sound-amplified parametric driving, a technique previously implemented only in traditional interferometers. Through numerical optimization, we demonstrate that this combined design surpasses both the conventional and standalone sloshing-Sagnac limits in sensitivity. Furthermore, when integrated into a network with Advanced LIGO, this proposed configuration—hereafter called the AXIOLIGO network—yields improved Bayesian routine sourcing, particularly for isotropic sensitivity curves closer to the AXIOLIGO characteristics and within directional sky regions where AXIOLIGO offers superior sensitivity to Advanced LIGO. Notably, an isotropic curve for the sloshing-sagnac/AXIOLIGO network approaching that of Advanced LIGO/Advanced LIGO+ results in roughly a 10% increase in Bayesian sourcing sensitivity compared to the current Advanced LIGO/Advanced LIGO+ setup. Additionally, we identify a "golden sensitivity region," a specific directional region where the sloshing-sagnac instrument exhibits significantly higher sensitivity than Advanced LIGO; in this zone, Bayesian sourcing for the AXIOLIGO network is expected to be even more robust. Finally, we discuss the feasibility of deploying this design as a network component and propose a near-term implementation plan within the context of the Indian-1 project. Our findings indicate that adopting an optically enhanced sloshing-Sagnac instrument could achieve a sensitivity improvement of approximately two orders of magnitude relative to current deployments. Such a drastic increase would undoubtedly transform gravitational-wave sourcing, directionality, and associated scientific investigations, warranting further exploration and potential deployment in a future third-generation interferometer.
Large-scale multiple-access XL-MIMO systems offer substantial gains in spectral efficiency and user-equitable resource allocation, making them ideal for dense urban environments and massive IoT deployments. However, the random access (NOVR) protocol in XL-MIMO often suffers from reduced performance due to overly wide effective pilot contending groups (EPCG) and prolonged pilot contamination contending groups (PCG). To address this, we developed a NOVR-XL formulation that incorporates angular, spatial, and beamforming filtering to enhance access group efficiency and reduce contamination. Furthermore, we introduced an improved variant called NOVR-XL+, which utilizes a two-phase protocol with an initial narrow pilot group (NPG) training stage followed by a data transmission phase. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed protocols significantly outperform the traditional NOVR-XL across various system parameters, particularly at high numbers of antenna arrays (NAAs) and access groups (AGs). Notably, in our specific simulation setup, the access success rate (ASR) and sum rate (SR) for the target user increased by 20x and 4x, respectively, when comparing NOVR-XL+ to NOVR-XL with 8 NAAs and 4 AGs. Finally, we conducted outdoor urban tests in a real-world scenario to validate the practicality of our proposed protocols. To push system performance even further, we formulated an optimal resource allocation strategy for NOVR-XL+, balancing access success rates and overall spectral efficiency. This optimization was achieved using a block coordinate descent algorithm, an efficient low-complexity method for determining transmit beamforming vectors and power control. Additionally, we evaluated the feasibility of a dynamic access success rate threshold to switch between NOVR and ordered access based on the expected ASR, ensuring feasible service levels for all access groups. Finally, we assessed the feasibility of adaptive multiuser detection (MUD) filtering as a successor to NOVR-XL+ for the most contended access groups. Our simulations confirm that both the optimal resource allocation and the MUD successor feasiblely improve system performance beyond the limits of NOVR-XL+.

Although neural language models have mostly outperformed $N$-gram models in performance, integrating an $N$-gram component with a neural component has become a standard technique for further boosting language model evaluation, enhancing machine translation, and improving textual entropy reduction. While previous studies primarily added $N$-grams as a standalone pre-component before a neural model, this work investigates inserting a unigram component between the embedding and first layers of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, and Transformer models. Our findings indicate that this mid-component approach yields only marginal improvements over using a unigram model separately with these architectures, failing to consistently surpass the best single-model performance. Consequently, while the mid-component method significantly benefits evaluation metrics, it offers limited benefits for machine translation and textual entropy reduction. In contrast, the traditional pre-component strategy remains highly effective, consistently beating other configurations across all models and tasks. Despite these contributions, determining the optimal position for a unigram component remains underexplored for Transformers, as our results show that a unigram pre-component yields no significant improvement when combined with a Transformer. Furthermore, this study confirms that increasing N-gram order provides minimal benefits, while expanding vocabulary size proves detrimental to model performance. Although recurrent and convolutional neural networks have been extensively utilized for sequence modeling, transformers have rapidly become the dominant architecture in natural language processing, surpassing both recurrent models and traditional statistical methods like $N$-grams. Notable examples of this trend include BERT and its variants (e.g., RoBERTa), which have set new benchmarks in various NLP benchmarks, and Transformer-based models that have significantly improved over standalone unigrams in sequence labeling. Despite these advances, there has been considerable research into whether adding an $N$-gram component—whether as a pre-, mid-, or post-component—can further enhance performance, with most earlier works focusing on recurrent and convolutional models rather than transformers.
This study presents an hybrid optical character recognition (H-OCR) vote tabulation system designed to accurately recognize and convert Indian multistate election votes into a correct digital format. The system integrates a deep learning-based spell correction algorithm with two H-OCR pipelines: one utilizing conventional methods and the other based on convolutional neural networks. Conventional noise patterns were identified from erroneous outputs generated by the initial H-OCR pipeline, which were then used to construct a deep learning-based noise removal algorithm. These two pipelines were sequentially connected, with the output from the traditional noise removal algorithm fed into the convolutional neural network-based H-OCR algorithm. Finally, the correct spelling of misrecognized words was inserted using a dynamic programming-based spell correction algorithm. Experimental results on a real-world Indian multistate election vote dataset, compared against ground truth, demonstrate that the proposed H-OCR system outperforms existing methods across all metrics. Specifically, the F1-score improved by 8.40%, the Levenshtein distance decreased by one unit, and both the mean square error and consensus accuracy showed significant enhancements. The algorithm's effectiveness and utility were validated on the actual Indian multistate election dataset to convert optical scanned vote data into digital format for correct vote tabulation. Furthermore, the system's application could benefit environmental noisy data datasets, such as those from seismography, medical CT scans, and forensic fingerprint analysis. The source code and dataset for the proposed system are accessible at https://github.com/Rajeshkumar078/H-OCR.
This study investigates the baroclinic storms on Mars, which exhibit circulation patterns reminiscent of those in an Earth-like atmosphere. Using a simplified two-layer model of the Martian atmosphere, we extend previous research by examining a broader range of physical parameters. Our analysis focuses on three key areas: (i) the linear growth rates and spatial structures of baroclinic instabilities, (ii) the development of non-linear vortex dipoles and zonal jets, and (iii) the formation of secondary vortices and higher-order jets. By comparing our outcomes to those from a model incorporating real atmospheric conditions, we identify similarities in how vortices and jets evolve on Mars. These findings highlight the fundamental processes governing baroclinic instability under both Martian and Earth-like scenarios. Notably, a single primary vortex dipole dominates the non-linear phase early on, followed by the emergence of secondary vortices and zonal jets at later stages, mirroring the lifecycle of a baroclinic eddy on Earth. Once these secondary features develop, various combinations of vortices and multijet structures can exist simultaneously, depending on specific physical parameters. The work described here serves as a foundational step toward understanding severe atmospheric events on Mars, such as global dust storms. To facilitate further investigation, our model code is accessible via GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ncapet/MarsStormModel. This resource can also support the planning of observations using instruments like the Perseverance rover and future missions, including the proposed Next-Generation Sounder for Mars.

At the turn of the 20th century, Weierstrass, Hilbert, and others introduced the concept of analytic continuation to resolve ambiguities arising from the multi-valued nature of special functions defined via integral representations along different Hankel contours. This issue was particularly evident with Euler's original definition of the Gamma function. Recently, the author developed a novel "Hankel calculus" employing elementary deformation rules, which enabled the direct manipulation and derivation of integral representations without invoking analytic continuation. These methods yielded new results and simplified existing proofs of various identities and integral forms of special functions that had previously been derived through cumbersome analytic continuation techniques or other cumbersome approaches. Recently, these Hankel calculus methods were extended to Riemann sheets of complexity beyond two, utilizing a generalized concept of deformation. In this survey, the author outlines these methods and highlights recent applications, while also addressing open questions and proposing new directions. The revised Hankel calculus methods are particularly valuable for teaching and learning, as they rely on elementary concepts and straightforward rules, making them suitable for calculus-level instruction. The phenomenon of contextual variance, where a single word exhibits different lemma choices across sentences, has recently been shown to correct adverse semantic drift in Vietnamese-Vernacular English (VTE) pairs. This study investigates whether varying the intensity of contextual variance between source and target languages yields similar correction effects. Using a dataset of VTE parallel sentences, we systematically modified the lemma mapping in a subset to create versions with higher variance, then evaluated various inference-based neural machine translation systems on the resulting split data. Our findings indicate that increasing contextual variance does not consistently produce significant improvements in system performance. Furthermore, when assessed on standard development and test sets, both the original and high-variance dataset versions yielded nearly identical translation quality, with no statistically significant differences observed. When comparing these results to a similarly constructed Vietnamese-Indian English (IE) dataset, we conclude that semantic alignment between VTE source and target pairs in this specific dataset is sufficiently robust that emphasizing contextual variance does not enhance translation quality. This insight may help explain why systems overfit to the VTE development and test sets during training on this set. Overall, these results suggest that simply increasing contextual variance is not a universally effective strategy for improving neural machine translation. Moreover, before investing resources into collecting larger high-variance datasets, researchers should first validate its efficacy on a smaller set like the VTE semantic alignment dataset presented here. Future work could explore whether combining contextual variance with other techniques, such as multi-task learning, would yield better outcomes. Regarding the VTE semantic alignment dataset itself, despite its limited size, it has already proven valuable for developing and comparing systems for various downstream applications, including neural machine translation, statistical semantic role labeling, and contextual word representation learning. Given its potential, we recommend further utilizing this dataset on downstream tasks to verify its effectiveness. Finally, applying this approach to other language pairs could reveal whether their source-target semantic alignment is strong enough to forgo emphasis on contextual variance, or if their datasets require it to achieve optimal performance.

We introduce a novel approach to phonocardiogram (PCG) anomaly detection that functions effectively in noisy environments without needing patient-specific training data. This method leverages a pre-trained neural network on clean, labeled normal PCGs to detect anomalies in noisy, unknown samples. First, we extract time-frequency features from raw PCGs using a short-time Fourier transform (STFT), which are then fed into a convolutional autoencoder (CAE) trained solely on normal recordings in noise-free conditions. Second, to operate in noisy settings, we extract time-domain statistical features from the latent representations of the CAE to train a support vector machine (SVM) classifier on both normal and abnormal samples. This hybrid framework—combining time-frequency and time-domain statistical features with a CAE-SVM model—is evaluated using three public datasets: CMU, Shahrekhdai, and a new collection gathered in noise-filled environments. Results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing techniques across all public datasets, achieving F-score improvements of 5.31%, 7.54%, and 3.21% for the CMU, Shahrekhdai, and 3R-PCG datasets, respectively, confirming its superiority in detecting cardiac abnormalities via raw PCGs in noisy conditions. To facilitate future research, we also make the new 3R-PCG dataset publicly available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3QXUQ. The core contributions of this work include:
*   Development of a significant other contribution (not specified) to address a key gap, potentially enabling new applications or advancing the field.
*   Validation of the approach's effectiveness on multiple public PCG datasets, with the establishment of a new public dataset to support future studies.
*   Conduct of extensive experiments across various datasets, including private datasets like the 3R-PCG, to verify the method's reliability and consistency.

While the $^{3}-_{2}$ line intensity correlates strongly with total star formation rate (SFR), the ratio R1 ($^{3}-_{2}$/$^{2}-_{1}$) drops below unity in the most luminous galaxies due to subthermal excitation caused by rising gas densities and thermal coupling with the intense radiation field. Conversely, the R2 ratio ($^{2}-_{1}$/CI-H$\gamma$) remains largely independent of LIR, reflecting gas fraction variations. Using this framework, we re-evaluated the evidence for low-density molecular winds and circumgalactic gas in a sample of galaxies with LIR > 10$^{12}$L$_{\odot}$. For the most luminous systems, both R1 and R2 show strong positive correlations with log(SFR), mirroring findings from a broader dataset. However, we argue that the evidence for molecular winds in our sample is weak, and the high R1 values are more plausibly attributed to significant metallicities and large total gas reservoirs. Instead, we propose that elevated R2 results from low molecular gas fractions, likely caused by prior extensive star formation and associated chemical enrichment of the hot circumgalactic medium. These conclusions are supported by comparative analyses of CI, dust, and atomic hydrogen observations among ultra-diffuse, starburst, and normal main-sequence galaxies at similar scales. Ultimately, future investigations into massive galaxy gas cycles should prioritize direct measurements of molecular, atomic, and dust masses over reliance on indirect tracers like the CI fine-structure line.

However, fitting procedures often yield biological parameters that lack feasible interpretations. This study introduces an approach that integrates biological feasibility directly into the fitting process. This constraint takes the form of a polyhedral region derived from linear inequalities applicable to both direct and indirect biological featurities. This technique is easily implemented within standard Bayesian fitting software and offers substantial value during the early development stages of new differential models. By ensuring estimates remain biologically meaningful, researchers can skip the labor-intensive post-processing step required to filter out infeasible parameter estimates. Furthermore, this approach enhances predictive accuracy for new data, making it particularly useful for time-critical responses to emerging animal disease outbreaks. Multinational enterprises and online users often deal with data in various languages, making cross-lingual tasks essential for maximizing the use of multilingual resources. This study investigates how models trained solely on single-lingual structured data can be adapted to perform tasks using data from a different target language. Specifically, we address the challenge of utilizing unstructured text in a target language to classify sentiments into predefined labels learned from a source language. To address this, we propose a method leveraging multilingual language models to extract semantic relationships between the source and target languages, thereby learning a cross-lingual sentiment classification model. Extensive experiments using multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves cross-lingual sentiment classification performance comparable to methods that rely on independent text representation models for each language. Furthermore, our method outperforms a baseline model trained on a multi-task loss over both source and target datasets by approximately one percentage point in accuracy. Notably, these benefits are achieved without accessing the target language dataset multiple times, as is common in standard supervised learning, and without using any labeled target language data for training. Additionally, our approach requires no neural network architecture adjustments for the target language and remains effective even when source and target datasets differ significantly in size. Ultimately, these findings suggest that leveraging semantic relationships between languages allows for effective cross-lingual sentiment classification, offering a cost-efficient solution for utilizing text resources in underrepresented languages. Deepfake audio and video represent a significant threat to society, with the volume of deepfake content anticipated to rise by 600% over the next decade. This surge, coupled with the heterogeneous nature of fake news across modalities like text, audio, and video, makes it difficult to effective leverage existing detection models designed for single modality content. To address this challenge, we introduce FEND (Federation for Newstream Deepfake Detection), a system that enables multi-modality fake news detection without accessing raw data. Our approach utilizes the MetaFEND model, developed through a three-member collaborative framework consisting of two edge devices and one server. This system incorporates a dynamic graph convolutional network to extract features from heterogeneous content and employs a split training strategy to balance detection efficiency and accuracy. Extensive experiments using the Facebook fake news dataset confirm that MetaFEND achieves detection performance comparable to centralised deep learning models. Furthermore, these results demonstrate that meta learning, when applied in this distributed manner, is effective for detecting deepfake audio and video content. The source code for FEND is available at: https://github.com/NgoDiepLine/FEND.

This paper introduces a previously untested CNN architecture, the Fractional Convolutional Neural Network (FCNN), and evaluates its performance against conventional CNNs through various convolutional and fully connected layers. The primary objective of this study is to enhance the segmentation of regions of interest in medical imaging. Using a dataset of 2D CT scans for lung cancer patients sourced from the PLOS ONE repository (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0129932), the evaluated FCNN architecture achieved a segmentation accuracy of 99.1%, an IoU of 89.3%, and an F1 score of 92.5%. Additionally, the approach demonstrates the ability to reduce noise in images contaminated with salt-and-pepper noise. We introduce a unified framework for feature extraction that integrates an image generator with a representation learner. Initially, the system is trained using unsupervised feature extraction, during which the image generator and representation learner are successively updated. Subsequently, the network proceeds to supervised feature extraction, continuing the successive update process for both the image generator and representation learner until convergence is achieved. To our knowledge, this is the initial work to incorporate image generators into unsupervised representation learning and to demonstrate that such generators enhance representation quality before supervised learning begins. Extensive experiments on three standard datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach. Knowledge graphs (KGs) serve as structured repositories of real-world entities and their interconnections, playing a crucial role in diverse applications like intelligent search systems and biomedical research. Recently, there has been significant effort to utilize knowledge-based data—such as triples and tables—for training language models (LMs). This approach has led to the development of powerful KG-aware LMs capable of understanding semantic relationships between entities. These models have demonstrated superior performance over traditional text-based LMs in natural language understanding (NLU) tasks, particularly factual ones such as entity linking and factual question answering (FQA). Despite this success, there remains a gap in research regarding which specific linguistic features these models have learned from knowledge-based corpora. In this work, we conduct comprehensive experiments to identify the linguistic characteristics of factual datasets that enable models to master FQA. Our analysis reveals that models trained on triples do not rely on specific syntactic or semantic properties of those triples for success in FQA tasks. Instead, they achieve high accuracy by memorizing dataset entries, a strategy facilitated by excessive overfitting and the underutilization of contextual context. Surprisingly, we find that a simple regularization technique applied during pretraining on textual corpora effectively counteracts this overfitting, resulting in models that perform comparably to those trained on triples. Furthermore, this regularization yields additional benefits: it enhances the model's ability to locate mentions within knowledge-free corpora and improves its generalization onto unknown test sets. Ultimately, our study underscores the necessity of balancing the data sources used for training language models.
We employ the non-linear Yang-Mills (NYM) charge parameter within the framework of non-linear Yang-Mills-Dillon (NYMD) theory to investigate the thermal profiles and apparent horizons of NYMD black holes. We define the NYM shadow radius and construct the corresponding NYM shadow image, while also creating both NYM and linear Yang-Mills (LYM) $T-\rho$ (temperature-radius) profiles. The analysis highlights that the non-linearity parameter $b$ significantly influences the apparent horizon radius, the thermal profile shape, and the NYM shadow image. Specifically, increasing the non-linearity generally enlarges the apparent horizon radius and flattens the thermal profile. Conversely, increasing the charge parameter $\nu$ has the opposite effect. Unlike LYM black holes, NYM black holes exhibit a triple-point structure in their $T-\rho$ profiles. Furthermore, because the non-linear charge distribution extends further than the linear distribution, the NYM shadow radius is consistently larger than the LYM radius for identical mass and charge values. Finally, we derive phase diagrams for the NYM apparent horizon radius and the shadow radius.
The concept of optical entanglement modification—specifically, how nonclassical features of light alter upon passing through a material—is linked to nonclassical transformations of optical tomograms. This study introduces a method to generate two- and three-level entanglement degradation effects within optical tomograms, serving as a novel technique for visualizing nonclassical property changes in light. We demonstrate that fragmentation and the emergence of negative probabilities in probabilities and squares of probabilities serve as clear indicators of entanglement modification. Furthermore, we show how these phenomena can be used to detect nonclassical characteristics in transmitted intensity, quadrature, and EPR correlations. Additionally, the approach offers insights into the origin of entanglement modification, potentially revealing classical mechanisms, such as interference between classical waves. As a consequence, optical tomograms provide an effective tool for distinguishing between classical and nonclassical causes of entanglement change in transmitted light. Regarding the nonclassicality of transmitted light, we find that while optical effect temperatures (representing the strength of nonclassicality in intensity) and quadrature effect temperatures (quadrature nonclassicality) suggest nonclassicality in the transmitted light's intensity and quadratures, this does not necessarily imply nonclassicalness in the transmission coefficient. Surprisingly, however, EPR effect temperatures confirm the nonclassical nature of the transmission coefficient itself. Friction effects are also observed regarding the nonclassicality of the transmission coefficient. Consequently, optical tomograms emerge as a powerful method for characterizing nonclassicality and entanglement modification in the transmission coefficient and the emitted quadrature. It is important to note that entanglement modification occurs independently of the nonclassicality of the transmitted light. As demonstrated through specific examples, this phenomenon can happen even with a classically correlated local state and a vacuum state. Ultimately, we conclude that entanglement modification is a purely quantum effect rooted in quantum interference, independent of classical wave phenomena like superposition and diffraction, and unrelated to the nonclassicality of the transmitted light. The proposed method for characterizing entanglement modification in polarized correlated light via optical tomograms is universally applicable to any quantum state and can be implemented using a simple experimental setup. Furthermore, this approach holds significant value for investigating nonclassical effects in the transmission coefficient and for developing quantum images of objects.
The collaboration LHCb has determined, for the first time, the branching fractions for a set of previously unobserved decay modes, as well as upper limits for several higher-energy photoproduction channels. These fractions are derived from the ratio of observed decay modes rather than from absolute cross-section measurements; consequently, their uncertainties are systematics-driven and dominate at low mass points where statistical limits extend to $3\sigma$. An explicit decomposition of these uncertainties into statistical and systematic components is provided. Utilizing the measured branching fractions and their total uncertainties, the data are compared against predictions from the universal anomalous $WW\nu\nu$ coupling model, yielding no evidence for its existence within this photoproduction domain. Furthermore, the upper limits on the most suppressed decay modes demonstrate that, in these high-luminosity runs, these channels constitute a negligible source of $tt\to\gamma/\gamma^*+\ell/l\nu\nu\nu$ signal events.

Additionally, this tool can process any multiplicity free module defined by highest weight, facilitating similar constructions and analyses. Finally, we address the question of whether spectral reconstruction serves as a reliable method for determining the submodule lattice of any multiplicity free module.

Consequently, our findings suggest that future experiments with higher precision at low $q^2$, such as those planned by LHCb and Belle II, will be essential for definitively validating either framework. This study introduces an algorithm to construct the Lyapununov graph for piecewise smooth maps, specifically the tent map with an additional jump discontinuity. We construct this graph for the "trent" map—a combination of the tent and linear transformations—across various parameters. Notably, we identify that the Lyapunov exponent for the trent map follows the same pattern observed in the tent map. Furthermore, we construct the Lyapunov exponent curve for the trent map and its inverse curve to visualize how they evolve together. Finally, we construct the Lyapununov graph for the 3-trent map.

This research examines identifiability through the lens of Lyapunov exponents for the trent map. We define an $(n,\lambda)$-identifiable curve for the trent map and construct Lyapunov exponent curves to analyze its identifiability. Extending previous work on the tent map, we explicitly construct the Lyapunov exponent curve for the trent map $T_a \circ L_{\alpha_1} \circ L_{\alpha_2}$, where $0<a<1$ and $0,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,1$ are ordered. We derive a formula for this curve and verify it through numerical examples. Additionally, we prove that this constructed curve represents the unique Lyapunov exponent for the specified parameter settings. These findings provide clear insights into the Lyapunov exponent's behavior and its relationship with system identifiability. Finally, we explore the Lyapunov exponents of the $k$-trent map for $k\geq3$, establishing clear bounds and invariance properties.

Building on this bound, we propose TPC, a simplified framework for enhancing certified robustness for based PCMs versus twisting transformations. Extensive experiments using 20 diverse PCM models demonstrate that TPC significantly boosts certified robustness across various tested images and smoothing intensities when confronting twisting transformations. Specifically, for models with an underlying certified accurate rate (CAR) around 70%, TPC increases the PCM's CAR by approximately 2% to 5%. These findings indicate that adopting TPC before auditing yields significantly better outcomes than traditional methods. We introduce a novel, fully automated algorithm for interactive proof by decomposition, implemented within the ALCHEMI testing environment. Once corrections are made, the environment automatically re-runs the failing test case to verify that the issue has been addressed. If the cause description remains inaccurate or insufficiently specific, the algorithm assists in refining it further. To demonstrate the algorithm's utility and automate error reporting, we integrated ALCHEMI into the CICVS competitive programming platform, where teams utilize it to track and resolve issues related to verified theorems and lemmas. Our integration yielded 21 error reports; following our recommended corrections, these issues were verified and closed by the verification engineer. These results indicate that the refined error reporting process described here can significantly shorten the cycle required to identify, address, and confirm the resolution of problems between programmers and users. Additionally, this approach can enhance the reliability of certified software by ensuring that reported issues are genuine and that fixes are thoroughly validated before implementation. This paper details our integration process and presents a list of errors reported through this method during the CICVS 2023 contest, alongside their verification statuses. Furthermore, we describe the algorithm for precisely formulating root cause descriptions and offer guidelines for effective verified software development to optimize this process, which can be immediately applied.

Self-sensing composites offer the potential for damage detection through an embedded self-sensing actuation and reconstruction framework. However, accurate damage reconstruction from self-sensing signals demands extensive pre-calibration using boundary condition calibrations across a wide amplitude range, which is challenging to implement in real-world self-sensing composite applications. This study introduces a calibration-less damage detection method based on a genetic algorithm (GA). Utilizing Lamb waves, the proposed approach employs a calibration-less process to identify damage via a single excitation frequency and one reconstruction signal. After an initial damage detection to establish a vicinity range, the framework focuses on the reconstruction within that specific vicinity without altering the excitation frequency or mode, enabling accurate damage reconstruction without precise excitation amplitude. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy delivers precise damage reconstruction within the targeted vicinity, confirming that a calibration-less method using a single excitation frequency and condition is feasible for accurate damage reconstruction within a specified area. Furthermore, the GA-based calibration-less framework can be applied post-initial detection to continuously monitor damage growth without changing the excitation frequency or mode, ultimately providing accurate damage reconstruction without initial calibration. These capabilities suggest that this framework is suitable for damage detection and health monitoring using self-sensing actuation and reconstruction, supporting damage detection, initial assessment, and continuous health monitoring without extensive pre-calibration. Additionally, this approach can be utilized in low-frequency range applications, such as monitoring damage in wind turbine blade composites.
This paper introduces a novel approach to deriving new integral identities by applying geometric vector methods within complex analysis. These techniques are demonstrated to be effective for constructing integral representations of complex polynomials, offering an alternative to traditional algebraic methods. The applications include the development of a new proof for a multi-dimensional Cauchy integral formula and the establishment of integral formulas involving products of Line Integral Complex Functions (LICFs). These innovations provide fresh perspectives on problems previously addressed through algebraic techniques, such as separating real and imaginary components of LICFs and constructing integral representations for complex potentials in fluid dynamics. Additionally, the author presents a unified proof for Cauchy-type integral identities found in recent literature. The work concludes with suggestions for further research. These methodologies are implemented using the computer algebra system Maple, specifically via the author's package CommComplexGeoVectors available at https://github.com/ArXivAuto/ArXivAuto.git.

This study addresses the convergence rate of the Nested Neumann algorithm, specifically analyzing how the inception depth influences the rate up to logarithmic factors. While a limited inception depth is beneficial for achieving a rapid pre-asymptotic convergence, it is detrimental to the asymptotic convergence rate. The proposed proof technique employs a coupling argument, utilizing the monotonically improving property of the Neumann algorithm at the nesting level where inception occurs. Furthermore, the work presents a counter-example demonstrating that no upper bound on the inception depth can guarantee an asymptotic convergence rate of $O(1/n)$ without additional constraints. Finally, numerical experiments are included to validate the theoretical findings. These experiments also explore strategies to mitigate the detriment of high inception depths, comparing the Nested Neumann algorithm with Stochastic Gradient Descent for solving the block angular linear inverse problem. Notably, these results confirm that for this specific problem type, Gradient Descent methods remain effective even when gradients are computed via the Neumann approach. To facilitate replication, the code will be made accessible through the ArXiv source code repository. Mathematical subject classifications for this work are 90C25, 90C31, 90C22, and 90C26.
We address the fundamental trade-off between information gathering and utilization in contextual linear bandits, where an agent selects actions based on observed contexts to maximize cumulative context rewards over a fixed horizon. While optimal strategies generally depend on the specific context distribution, prior research shows that exploiting this distributional knowledge requires infinite bit communication when the context space is continuous. This work demonstrates that, by partitioning the continuous context space, one can approximate the optimal policy using finite bit communication. Furthermore, we propose a practical algorithm that exploits a known context distribution to select actions within a discrete set. Our method yields nearly optimal cumulative context rewards as if the specific context distribution were unknown, while utilizing a finite bit budget. Specifically, for a discrete action set of size $K$, a context space dimension of $d$, and $N$ total time steps, our algorithm requires an $O(d \log N)$ bit budget per step. Theoretical analysis confirms that this approach achieves a regret bound of $O(K \sqrt{N \log N} + N \epsilon_N)$, where $\epsilon_N$ represents the regret incurred due to limited bit constraints. Numerical experiments using a Unified Language Model indicate that our algorithm outperforms baseline methods that assume a uniform context distribution. Additionally, we apply this framework to a real-world problem involving dynamic electrical load balancing among data centers. By explicitly considering a non-uniform context distribution, our algorithm identifies load-balancing contexts more effectively than baselines, resulting in significant increases in total context rewards, which correspond to reduced energy waste in data centers.

Using an optically thin cooling model valid for our simulation parameters, we demonstrate that external cooling limits the expansion of intruding low-angular momentum gas and stabilizes the disk against fragmentation. We find that dust absorption enhances cooling in the outer regions, offsetting the cooling efficiency drop in the mid-plane as dust settles. In simulations with significant dust growth (maximum radius $R_{50}=10$ cm), cooling efficiency in the outer region ($R_{out}=200$ AU) becomes ten times greater than in simulations without settling/growth ($R_{50}=0$ cm). Enhanced cooling reduces the sound speed, increasing disk susceptibility to gravitational instabilities and spiral arm formation. However, our simulations show that reducing thermal support alone is insufficient to trigger gravitational collapse in our setup. Furthermore, radiation pressure from dust on the disk surfaces creates an effective horizontal support force, suppressing vertical instability and the development of $m=0$ modes. Ultimately, while dust settling and growth amplify external cooling, our simulations indicate that none of these mechanisms were strong enough to initiate gravitational collapse within our specific configuration. These findings suggest other physical processes, such as SAURON or $H_2$ cooling, might be required to drive fragmentation in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. To test this, we increased the external cooling rate artificially in one simulation, which did lead to disk fragmentation at 200 AU; however, this approach lacks physical basis and requires further investigation.

Building upon the work of Cheeger, Gueorguiev, and Lin, we establish a Polya-Hardy inequality, utilize it to derive a Liouville theorem stating that harmonic functions with subcritical growth are necessarily constant. Furthermore, we examine the asymptotic behavior of positive harmonic functions defined on the level sets with respect to the soliton's gradient. As a consequence, we prove a Liouville result for harmonic functions exhibiting at most polynomial growth. Additionally, as an application, we demonstrate that the regular part of the level sets of a non-trivially shrinking soliton forms a sequence of compact manifolds that converge asymptotically to an Einstein manifold. Finally, by leveraging these asymptotic properties, we derive a structural characterization for this class of solitons. Our findings indicate that, aside from the Gaussian soliton, the level sets of the non-trivially shrinking soliton are either spherical space forms or asymptotically so. Finally, we obtain a Poincare inequality and a mean value inequality, which together enable us to rederive the Liouville property for harmonic functions satisfying polynomial growth. We investigate the random walk (RW) method, a recent technique proposed to alleviate communication inefficiencies inherent in learning models from distributed datasets. In this approach, participants mitigate this inefficiency by selecting data samples based on a random walk over their local datasets rather than transmitting gradients from all samples as in standard stochastic gradient descent. While the RW method offers significant potential for reducing communication costs, its performance has historically been limited by high sampling rates and an extensive number of iterations. To address these constraints, we first derive new, optimized bounds for both the number of samples and iterations within the RW strategy, yielding a superior method with significantly enhanced performance. Furthermore, we propose an adaptive variant that dynamically adjusts the sampling probability; this version requires only a brief warm-up phase during which an optimal probability is estimated before being adopted for the remaining learning process. Our theoretical findings confirm that this adaptive method achieves near-optimal performance. These contributions are validated through new numerical results demonstrating the approach's effectiveness, its scalability, and its robustness against noisy data. Additionally, the code for our implementation is accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/HamedBarandiaran/RandomWalk.

This research presents a novel shared hardware architecture for both TTP (Tucker-Three-Point) and HTTP (Hierarchical-TTP) factorized LSTM models, designed to accelerate TRIM (Transformed-RF LLM) intelligent voice recognition systems. Unlike conventional tensor-decomposed models that rely on heavy-shared hardware for TTP decomposition, our proposed FDHT-LITT architecture utilizes a Finite-Depth-Tree (FDHT) structure to replace shared hardware units. This approach allows multiple TTP and HTTP LSTM models to be executed simultaneously without consuming additional hardware resources. Furthermore, the FDHT structure enables dynamic adaptation to varying numbers of shared models through a single tree, eliminating the need for hardware unit sharing. Integration of the FDHT with LITT architecture further optimizes execution efficiency by pruning unnecessary paths. Performance evaluations using realistic workloads demonstrate that the proposed FDHT-LITT design achieves superior throughput and energy efficiency compared to conventional shared TTP-based hardware. Furthermore, this architecture offers flexible throughput levels across different workloads without compromising area constraints or energy usage. These findings validate the FDHT-LITT approach as a viable solution for scaling LSTM-based TRIM model performance, potentially replacing complex shared TTP hardware configurations. These performance metrics align closely with our proposed FDHT-LITT architectural framework.
This paper presents an explicit version of the Chebotarev density theorem for function fields, established over $\F_q[t]$ where $q$ is not necessarily a power of a prime. The stated constants depend on $q$ and vanish as $q$ approaches infinity. We also provide explicit inequalities ensuring the validity of the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture within the domain of validity of our Chebotarev estimate; these inequalities are verified computationally for primes $2\le q\le 37$. These results extend those found in \cite{PR17}. Furthermore, we examine the analogue of Hilbert's irreducibility theorem in function fields, deriving an estimate for the number of non-irreducible polynomials of a specified degree, and we consider the problem of determining the Galois group for a product of two previously identified irreducible polynomials. Finally, we outline potential applications of these findings to the study of rational points on curves defined over $\F_q[t]$. In this context, we derive an explicit constant in Chevalley's theorem and offer an explicit statement of Lang's conjecture for this specific setting.
This paper addresses the fundamental issue of blow-up for solutions to the Schrödinger equation that encounter a boundary, a scenario where classical proof methods generally fail due to the loss of concentration energy in the limiting Sobolev function. We introduce a novel approach that bypasses this obstacle, enabling blow-up proofs for Schrödinger solutions. As applications of our new framework, we first establish the existence of blowing-up solutions for Schrödinger-Conformal Yang-Mills maps defined on the ball $B(0,1)$ in $\R^3$ and for Schrödinger-harmonic maps from $B(0,1)$ in $\R^2$ into a compact Riemannian manifold $\mathcal{N}$. Furthermore, utilizing the blow-up mechanism developed here, we derive a strong uniqueness result for weak solutions near the singularity and, by extension, a stable price-skewing property for the Schrödinger diffusion process.
We introduce a collection of operators designed to transfer statements from positive-characteristic $p$ back to characteristic-zero. These same operators enable the construction of a Liariv-Rotem derivative with respect to $p$ in the subalgebra of the polynomial algebra that is spanned by the monomials for which these derivatives remain non-zero. These concepts are applied to investigate Riemann-derived algebra structures, to define and analyze in positive-characteristic a set of conditions generalizing the Jordan derivative $f(t) = t^z - 1$ (where $z > 1$ is an integer) and the condition of being $n$-derived (for $n \geq 2$). Additionally, we define and study in positive-characteristic the notion of being characteristic-zero-derived, and we characterize algebra derivations that satisfy this property. Finally, we characterize idempotent derivations in positive-characteristic and demonstrate that any finite-dimensional subalgebra of a characteristic-zero-derived algebra that admits such a derivation must be trivial. The connections between these concepts and Lie-derived algebras are also discussed. These ideas further serve to clarify recent findings by the second author regarding derived and Lie-derived algebra structures in positive-characteristic that emerged from computer-generated counterexamples to long-standing conjectures in commutative algebra. Among the author's definitions, those relevant to characteristic-zero-derived algebras can be adapted to positive-characteristic $p$ to produce a complementary set of concepts in that context, potentially aiding in resolving open problems in commutative algebra regarding the failure of Lefschetz-type principles in characteristic-zero that have implications for algebra-derived structures. This potential utility is illustrated by characterizing in positive-characteristic $p$ the set of derivations that correspond to the Riemann derivative $f(t) = |t|^z \frac{d}{dt}$ for real numbers $z \geq 1$. This study introduces a novel approach for calibrating the cross-shaped focal plane detector (FPD) used in lobster-eye optics. This calibration was achieved by fitting a simple parametric arc model to the raw data, which includes an azimuthal angle and a spatial extent defined by the cone angle of the surrounding mirror tube array. As a result, a clearly segmented cross-like image emerges, where each segment's slope corresponds to the rotation angle of that specific FPD array segment. We demonstrate this technique using raw data from a 5x5 segmented FPD, which produced a cross image with four distinct segments reflecting the orientation of its mirror tube arrays. Furthermore, we employed this method to locate a hidden FPD array within the same dataset, which appeared as a small, previously unidentified arc segment. Finally, we applied this calibration method to a fully assembled 10x10 FPD, confirming its effectiveness and ease of use.
